name: Go goroutines (skynet 1M-spawn benchmark vs pthread/std::thread)
baseline: pthread_create and std::thread (C/C++ OS threads, 8 kB pthread stacks) running the skynet recursive spawn-and-sum benchmark
workload: skynet microbenchmark: a root unit spawns 10 children, each spawns 10 more, down to 1,000,000 leaves that return their ordinal; sums flow back up; time per spawned unit (goroutine versus OS thread).
claimed_speedup: Go (go1.8.1): 0.42-0.49 us per goroutine (average over 1,000,000) versus pthread 54-73 us and std::thread 52-73 us per thread (average over 10,000): about 110x-175x lower cost per unit (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C++ side: gcc-6.3.1, Boost.Build variant=release optimization=speed (pthreads created with 8 kB stacks); Go side: go1.8.1, flags not stated
hardware: dual Intel Xeon E5-2620 v4 2.2 GHz, 16C/32T, 64 GB RAM, Linux x86_64
tradeoffs: Goroutines run on the Go runtime's user-space scheduler with a garbage-collected heap and growable stacks; the cost is runtime size, GC pauses and no manual control of placement. Calling C from Go (cgo) is slower than a C call.
caveats: The baseline is OS threads (pthread_create, std::thread), not the idiomatic C++ answer for massive concurrency. The same page shows Boost.Fiber (C++ user-space fibers, work stealing, tcmalloc) at 0.05-0.09 us per fiber, which matches or beats Go and Erlang, so this is not a claim that the language beats well-tuned C++. Scale differs: the Go/Haskell/Erlang rows average over 1,000,000 spawned units while the pthread/std::thread rows average over only 10,000 threads because the 1,000,000-thread run exhausted resources (so the ratio compares per-unit cost at different sizes). The numbers come from the Boost.Fiber author's own documentation, ported skynet code for the C++ side (performance/thread/skynet_pthread.cpp: detached pthreads plus a mutex and condition-variable buffered channel) versus the upstream Go source's unbuffered channels; toolchains are from 2017 (go1.8.1, ghc-8.0.1, erts-8.3, gcc-6.3.1). Go/Haskell/Erlang compile flags and runtime options (for example GHC +RTS -N) are not stated on the page. The per-language skynet sources are in https://github.com/atemerev/skynet (MIT, last commit 2023-11-10). Tier B, not A, because the workload sizes differ and the non-C++ flags are unstated; rerunning at an equal unit count would settle it.
found_via: WebSearch: 'lightweight threads comparison goroutines vs pthreads creation time Go faster than C pthreads paper evaluation' surfaced the Boost.Fiber performance page; opened the .qbk source on github.com and the skynet repo.
why_faster: Implied by the page rather than argued: goroutines are user-space units scheduled by the Go runtime, while pthreads are OS threads (the 1,000,000-thread run exhausted resources). No explicit mechanism is given.

name: Erlang/OTP processes (skynet 1M-spawn benchmark vs pthread/std::thread)
baseline: pthread_create and std::thread (C/C++ OS threads, 8 kB pthread stacks) running the skynet recursive spawn-and-sum benchmark
workload: skynet microbenchmark: a root unit spawns 10 children, each spawns 10 more, down to 1,000,000 leaves that return their ordinal; sums flow back up; time per spawned unit (Erlang process versus OS thread).
claimed_speedup: Erlang (erts-8.3): 0.63-0.73 us per process (average over 1,000,000) versus pthread 54-73 us and std::thread 52-73 us per thread (average over 10,000): about 74x-116x lower cost per unit (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C++ side: gcc-6.3.1, Boost.Build variant=release optimization=speed (pthreads created with 8 kB stacks); Erlang side: erts-8.3, flags not stated
hardware: dual Intel Xeon E5-2620 v4 2.2 GHz, 16C/32T, 64 GB RAM, Linux x86_64
tradeoffs: BEAM processes have private heaps and communicate by copying messages; per-process GC, no shared mutable state, and a VM that is slower than C for numeric code.
caveats: The baseline is OS threads (pthread_create, std::thread), not the idiomatic C++ answer for massive concurrency. The same page shows Boost.Fiber (C++ user-space fibers, work stealing, tcmalloc) at 0.05-0.09 us per fiber, which matches or beats Go and Erlang, so this is not a claim that the language beats well-tuned C++. Scale differs: the Go/Haskell/Erlang rows average over 1,000,000 spawned units while the pthread/std::thread rows average over only 10,000 threads because the 1,000,000-thread run exhausted resources (so the ratio compares per-unit cost at different sizes). The numbers come from the Boost.Fiber author's own documentation, ported skynet code for the C++ side (performance/thread/skynet_pthread.cpp: detached pthreads plus a mutex and condition-variable buffered channel) versus the upstream Go source's unbuffered channels; toolchains are from 2017 (go1.8.1, ghc-8.0.1, erts-8.3, gcc-6.3.1). Go/Haskell/Erlang compile flags and runtime options (for example GHC +RTS -N) are not stated on the page. The per-language skynet sources are in https://github.com/atemerev/skynet (MIT, last commit 2023-11-10). Tier B, not A, because the workload sizes differ and the non-C++ flags are unstated; rerunning at an equal unit count would settle it. In the upstream skynet README the Erlang run needs erl +P 2000000 to raise the process limit; that option is not mentioned on the Boost.Fiber page.
found_via: WebSearch: 'lightweight threads comparison goroutines vs pthreads creation time Go faster than C pthreads paper evaluation' surfaced the Boost.Fiber performance page; the Erlang row is on the same page.
why_faster: Implied by the page rather than argued: Erlang processes are lightweight units scheduled by the BEAM, pthreads are OS threads. No explicit mechanism is given.
